title: Electron sharing reactions
source: Questions and terms copied unchanged from the site's bank, except where marked for IB Diploma Chemistry (status of the source: ai-reviewed-reverified-gate-verified-2026-09-30-awaiting-human-signoff). Terms and clues: R3.3#c01 bank term, clue written for the game from the bank's definition; R3.3#c07 bank term, clue written for the game from the bank's definition; R3.3#c03 bank term, clue written for the game from the bank's definition; R3.3#c06 bank term, clue written for the game from the bank's definition. Questions: R3.3#q01, R3.3#q03, R3.3#q06, R3.3#q02, R3.3#q04, R3.3#q07, R3.3#q05, R3.3#q08, R3.3#q09, R3.3#q10.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Radical
items.clue: A species with an unpaired electron.

items.label: Termination steps
items.clue: Stages in which two reactive species combine, ending chains.

items.label: Homolytic fission
items.clue: A covalent bond breaks so that each atom takes one electron of the pair.

items.label: Propagation steps
items.clue: Stages in which one reactive species is consumed and another is produced.

options.text: A molecular entity that has an unpaired electron
A molecular entity that carries an electric charge
A group of atoms that stays together in reactions
A molecular entity with an incomplete octet

questions.explanation: This is the definition: a radical has an unpaired electron, as in •CH₃ and Cl•. The unpaired electron is what makes radicals highly reactive.

questions.stem: Methane reacts with bromine in ultraviolet (UV) light. Which equation represents the initiation step?

options.text: Br₂ → Br⁺ + Br⁻
CH₄ → •CH₃ + H•
Br₂ → Br• + Br•
CH₄ → CH₃⁻ + H⁺

questions.explanation: UV light supplies the energy to break the Br–Br bond homolytically: one electron of the bonding pair goes to each atom, giving two bromine radicals. The Br–Br bond is much weaker than a C–H bond, so it is the bond that breaks.

questions.stem: Cyclohexane reacts with chlorine in UV light. Which equation represents a propagation step of this reaction?

options.text: C₆H₁₂ + Cl• → C₆H₁₁Cl + H•
•C₆H₁₁ + Cl₂ → C₆H₁₁Cl + Cl•
•C₆H₁₁ + Cl• → C₆H₁₁Cl
C₆H₁₂ + Cl⁺ → C₆H₁₁Cl + H⁺

questions.explanation: A propagation step has one radical on each side: •C₆H₁₁ reacts with a Cl₂ molecule to form chlorocyclohexane and a new Cl• radical, which carries the chain on. The other propagation step is C₆H₁₂ + Cl• → •C₆H₁₁ + HCl.

questions.stem: Which species is a radical, and for what reason? Any charge on a species is shown, but unpaired electrons are not marked.

options.text: BF₃, because boron has only 6, not 8, outer-shell electrons
C₂H₅, because it has an odd number (13) of valence electrons
OH⁻, because it has one more electron than a neutral OH group
Cl₂, because it reacts vigorously with many substances

questions.explanation: Count the valence electrons: 2 × 4 + 5 × 1 = 13. An odd number of electrons cannot all be paired, so one is unpaired: this is the ethyl radical, •C₂H₅ (usually written •CH₂CH₃).

questions.stem: In the homolytic fission of Cl₂, two single-barbed (fish-hook) arrows are drawn, each starting at the Cl–Cl bond and ending at a different chlorine atom. What does each arrow represent?

options.text: The movement of an electron pair
The movement of a chlorine atom
The release of stored bond energy
The movement of one electron

questions.explanation: A single barb means one electron. Each arrow moves one electron of the Cl–Cl bonding pair to a different chlorine atom, so each atom becomes Cl•.

questions.stem: A student claims: 'Chlorine radicals are used up in the propagation steps, so every molecule of CH₃Cl formed from methane and chlorine needs a new Cl• from the initiation step.' Which evaluation of this claim is correct?

options.text: Incorrect: the H• formed in the first step reacts with Cl₂ to re-form Cl• for the chain
Correct: each propagation step uses up a radical, so each CH₃Cl needs a new initiation
Correct: CH₃Cl forms when •CH₃ and Cl• combine, which uses up two radicals each time
Incorrect: the Cl• used in the first step is re-formed in the second, so it can react again

questions.stem: Methane and chlorine react in UV light or on heating. Bond enthalpies: Cl–Cl 242 kJ mol⁻¹; C–H 414 kJ mol⁻¹. Which bond breaks in the initiation step, and why?

options.text: C–H breaks, because breaking the stronger bond releases the greater amount of energy
Cl–Cl breaks, because the bond splits readily into Cl⁺ and Cl⁻ ions
Cl–Cl breaks, because less energy is needed to break it than to break C–H
C–H breaks, because the alkane must lose an H atom before chlorine can react

questions.explanation: Breaking a bond requires energy equal to its bond enthalpy. The Cl–Cl bond (242 kJ mol⁻¹) needs far less than the C–H bond (414 kJ mol⁻¹), so UV light or heat breaks Cl–Cl homolytically: Cl₂ → 2Cl•.

questions.stem: The products of the reaction of methane with chlorine in UV light include CH₂Cl₂, CHCl₃ and CCl₄. How are most of these more highly substituted products formed?

options.text: Cl• removes an H atom from a chloromethane; the radical then reacts with Cl₂
Cl• replaces an H atom in a chloromethane directly, releasing a free H• radical
Chlorinated methyl radicals combine with Cl• in termination, the main source of products
Each forms in one step, e.g. CH₃Cl + Cl₂ → CH₂Cl₂ + HCl, as its equation shows

questions.explanation: Cl• attacks C–H bonds in chloromethanes as it does in methane, e.g. CH₃Cl + Cl• → •CH₂Cl + HCl, then •CH₂Cl + Cl₂ → CH₂Cl₂ + Cl•. Repeating these propagation steps gives CHCl₃ and CCl₄.

questions.stem: A small amount of ethane, C₂H₆, is found in the product mixture when methane reacts with chlorine in UV light. Which statement explains why ethane is present?

options.text: A methyl radical replaces H in methane: •CH₃ + CH₄ → C₂H₆ + H•
A methyl cation and methyl anion combine: CH₃⁺ + CH₃⁻ → C₂H₆
Two methyl radicals combine in a termination step: •CH₃ + •CH₃ → C₂H₆
It is not a reaction product; only CH₃Cl and HCl form, so it is an impurity

questions.explanation: In termination any two radicals combine. When two •CH₃ radicals meet, their unpaired electrons pair to form a C–C bond, giving ethane. Such collisions are rare, so only a little ethane forms.

questions.stem: Alkanes react with very few reagents. Which statement explains the low reactivity of alkanes?

options.text: Their C–C and C–H bonds are strong and are essentially non-polar.
They are saturated, and saturated compounds are unreactive.
Each atom has a full outer shell, so the molecule is unreactive.
Strong intermolecular forces hold the molecules together.

questions.explanation: Strong bonds need a large energy input to break, and because carbon and hydrogen have similar electronegativities the bonds have no significant partial charges for polar reagents to attack.
